newsitem.title: USA: ABA president backs tough pay-to-play ban on lwyrs.
newsitem.headline: ABA president backs tough pay-to-play ban on lwyrs.

text.p: American Bar Association President Lee Cooper said Wednesday he backs a rule proposed by the Association of the Bar of the City of New York to ban "pay-to-play" by lawfirms with municipal bond practices.

Cooper's comments during an interview with Reuters came one day before Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Arthur Levitt is set to announce a committee of prominent lawyers that plans to urge ABA shortly to condemn the practice as an ethics violation.

"I am opposed to anything that would give the appearance of impropriety," said Cooper, whose association is expected to debate the issue at its annual meeting in San Francisco in August. "I personally would support a prohibition."
Raymond Trombadore, chairman of ABA's standing committee on professional discipline, said Wednesday that his panel has adopted a tough resolution condemning pay-to-play.

"We think it's a real problem. We think we should find ways to deal with this practice," said Trombadore, a partner with Trombadore, Seel & Trombadore. He said the panel has offered to work with the New York City bar to develop a "balanced" resolution on the issue.
The New York City bar's rule says if a lawyer contributes to a municipal issuer official, then the attorney's firm could not conduct public finance business with that bond issuer for two years.
The Trombadore panel says ABA "decries the practice of lawyers making or soliciting contributions to public officials in order to be retained by public agencies for professional regulatory services."
The panel says ABA should "encourage state legislatures and other regulatory agencies to adopt appropriate rules and policies to prevent public officials from participating in this practice."
ABA should urge courts and regulators to enforce ethical standards and rules of professional conduct that prohibit the practice, the panel adds.

Meanwhile, a panel representing seven ABA committees and sections has called for creation of a task force to investigate the issue and report to ABA's House of Delegates with recommendations in August 1998.

Peter Moser, head of the joint panel, said the group recommends condemning pay-to-play in the muni area and is studying how ABA can tackle the problem for any lawyer that does work for state and local governments - not just muni lawyers.
"We think it is part of a broader problem" than just the municipal bond bar, said Moser, a partner with Piper & Marbury in Baltimore.

Levitt is expected to announce Thursday that William Webster, former chief of the Central Intelligence Agency, will head the lawyers' panel that plans to lobby ABA on pay-to-play. Webster was unavailable for comment.
